comments.text:
The average annual price increase for MSRP actually isn’t that bad. It’s more than average inflation but not much more. The MSRP has increased an average of 5.6% per year since 2014. The bigger issue is the market price increase. In 2014, GTX graphics cards could be found for MSRP and were often on sale for less than MSRP. Since the 3080 series the difference between MSRP and the actual market price has increased substantially. 

Since 2020, RTX cards have been selling for 2 to 3 times MSRP for 24 months until the next series comes out. The cards are usually selling 3 times MSRP for the first 6 months and then slowly come down to 2 times MSRP from 6 to 12 months post launch, and then remain there until the next gen cards come out 24 months after launch. If we could buy a 5080 for $999 and a 5090 for $1,999, it wouldn’t be so bad. Right now, I can’t find a new 5090 for less than $2,899 and most of the better 5090s are still selling for $3,000 to $4,500. That’s insane!
comments.author: @ericandi

comments.text: It’s insane that the 5090 and 5080 cards are still selling for so much over MSRP a year after they launched. There still isn’t enough inventory and resellers are getting most of it and then jacking up the price.

comments.text:
Given that the 2080 Super came out just 6 months after the 2080, with more performance for less money, I am surprised you did not use the 2080 Super for the graph as being "more representative" of that particular release. 
Yet the 4080 Super IS included, despite making very little difference over a 16 month gap. 
It feels like the 2080 was "cherry picked" for being a particularly bad example, when it was QUICKLY remedied by nVidia at that time. 

As someone who bought into the 2080 at release, getting a 15% launch discount (when has THAT happened since 2018?), I have NOT been disappointed by that purchase.

In fact, my 7 year old card was just donated to a good cause, uplifting someone from a 1050ti  (it gives 3x the framerate in benchmark tests, keeping up with the 3k monitor he got as a Christmas present). 
That recipient has now passed on his 1050ti to a friend stuck with integrated graphics. 

I like the idea that no modern graphics card, no matter how "crappy", is still useful and valuable to someone. 

I'm now looking at reusing my late brother's 970 card to rebuild the 1050ti machine, so that the 2080 user's younger brother can inherit his old machine. 
From what I can see, the older generation card is about a match because of the higher class of gpu. 
And it's a ten year old graphics card... with only 4Gb of video ram, but then, so was the 1050ti. 
Obviously these cards will be limited to 1080p max, and reduced textures and detail at that. But they do still have a use, and don't deserve to be in landfill (or recycled) just yet. 

That seven year old 2080 is now performing admirably in Forza and Flight Sim... Old, but still a (gamer) life-changing upgrade.

comments.text:
I just don't think we're going to see as big of technological leaps going forward. We're already around 3nm which is about the physical limit before quantum effects become a huge problem. An atom is around .5 nm or smaller, and quantum tunneling can become a problem around 3nm. So what's next? I think the logical next step is to make what we already have more efficient and develop new techniques beside shrinking arcatechture. 

If NVIDIA or anyone else can improve things like frame gen to have near zero latency, and improve upscaling to be almost indistinguishable from rasterized frames, then I think it would be an acceptable path forward. DLSS and frame gen have both improved over time, so I don't see why it can't be perfected.

comments.text:
1080 - high end at a reasonable high end price.
2080 - high end with a bloated price tag because of them using DLSS and Ray tracing as a gimmicky selling point.
3080 - high end at a theoretical good value, but got scalped like crazy because of the crypto and covid bs.
4080 - high end at a bad price, not any better value than the 3080 for the price to performance, and relied on frame gen as a gimmick to help justify the price.
5080 - high end at a better but still bad price over the 4080. Barely provides any meaningful improvements and uses the multi-frame gen as a gimmick to justify the price and "performance" charts over the 4080.

NVIDIA's marketing over the years has gotten a lot more reliant on gimmicky or situational features for their claimed performance improvements to convince people to spend too much money on products that should be selling for hundreds of dollars less than they do, all while giving us less and less uplifts in pure performance from generation to generation. At this point, the 6080 is probably gonna be marketed as a card that's capable of running games at 4K at hundreds of FPS "with the power of DLSS 5", when the feature set is wanting you to use aggressive upscaling, multiple instances of frame gen to make your game look smoother while having poor latency as well as ghosting and smearing on the visuals, and giving your card just barely enough VRAM to get you to the next generation when you'll just pay them another $1,000+ for a GPU that's maybe 12% better than what you already have.

The problem is the Halo draws way too much wattage, even the connector cannot really withstand the heat of the transfer because the wires and pins are too small a gauge to support it safely, 600watts is too much for the connector from an engineering standpoint(that goes for the contact surface of the pins), and its too expensive for what it really is, grant it its a replacement for the Titan series that started out a Hybrid solution for CCs that was basically half Workstation and half Gaming card. comments.text:
3:00 I don't think this narrative holds up.
Nvidia's pricing strategy doesn't exist in a vacuum. The speed at which new microchip manufacturing rolled out has also greatly slowed down.
This is exactly why Nvidia has bet on Ray Tracing and AI upscaling/frame gen. The industry already knew that rasterised performance gains were about to hit severe diminshing returns.

AMD also has struggled with this. While they offer good rasterised performance for money, their power efficiency actually sucks. They flat out can't offer 4090-scale cards like this, nor eek out that much more rasterised performance out of their existing architectures. Their next gen will also only improve rasterised performance marginally and focus on RT, as well as abandon the high-end tiers.

The 5000 series is primarily a product of the fact that we're still limited to TSMC 4 nm (like the 4000 series) and that architectures are already so optimised that improvements in this direction accomplish very little. 10 years ago, you could improve efficiency within the same manufacturing process... now we already have all of the optimisations and acceleration structures in place that we can fit onto them.

The next big leaps will be in software/drivers to exploit the architectural features Nvidia has introduced over the past gens. Mega Geometry (a better Nanite for dynamic LOD meshes that's also super compatible with raytracing and may make alpha cutouts obsolete for many use cases) and Neural Rendering (greatly improved multi-layered shading at reduced texture sizes) look genuinely awesome.

comments.text: Want to add a bit to the discussion. Both 4080 super and 5080 are manufactured on the same node with the same chip area (1 mm^2 difference which is less than 1% area diff). I don't know why nvidia decided to use 5 nm 4N process again as I don't know the prices, it might be that on other nodes (4 nm or 3 nm) it wasn't feasible to manufacture a large amount of chips right now or the prices were unappealing or nvidia was just greedy to bump their margins. But you might already see where it is going - everything about these chips is almost identical - amount of transistors and therefore cores within 5% range and same cache. Same VRAM with the same amount of chips = the same bus. The only thing that differs any significantly is the VRAM generation (GDDR6x vs GDDR7) and frequency bumped by 30%, resulting in 30% higher bandwidth as everything else stays the same. If not this change, we would get the same card for the same price. Considering this, the power efficency gains are impressive and they are coming mostly from not directly GPU related stuff (software, other electrical improvements) as despite higher TDP (320W vs 360W), 5080 usually uses less power.

comments.text:
I am ride or die Team Green. Since my first TNT in 1998, I have bought 22 GPUs (even before GPU was a word) since then through my current 4080. I bought a mere 10 shares of NVDA at IPO and held them as they split and gained value to the point I sold half my holdings in 2021and paid off my mortgage 27-1/2 years early. My remaining shares have since grown 6X and were 7X before the DeepSeek scam-prompted crash. Nvidia has been very very good to me.

That said, Jensen needs to stop needing a fresh leather jacket every day because their products have become massively overpriced and now can't even point to massive gen over gen uplift in performance to justify the ridonkulous prices. With AMD giving up (as they should, cuz they've NEVER been as good), there's no competition to force price sanity. Nvidia has entered their Fat Elvis stage because they've gotten so rich off of AI and crypto before it, they don't even need us pesky gamers to make bank. What was once their core is now their charity business.

I came across the parts/price list for a rig I built in 2005: It cost about $1500 and the GPU, a 7800GT, cost $300 or 20% of the total. From roughly 2002 through 2015, my rigs cost ~$1500 for everything - case, PSU, mobo, CPU, GPU, HDD/SDD, etc. (excluding monitor, KB+M, etc.) - and while that money got you more RAM, bigger drives, more cores, faster speeds, the price was constant.

In Feb. 2023 I built my current rig to replace the 7-1/2 year-old one and while I decided to move up to a S-tier rig for video editing & all sliders right gaming, the price was over $2700 (before tax!) and that was with massive Bargain Ninja® shopping for open box components, bundles, discounts, etc. which saved over $1100 meaning someone paying full price would've spent nearly $4000. I was insanely lucky to snag an RTX 4080 for $830 (open box Best Buy w/a lot of Reward Zone credit), but even at the great discount that was 30% of the premium rig's cost.

After five years of ruinous Trump-Bidenflation when eggs which used to be a buck a dozen are now $5+, rent, gas, everything are expensive as hell, Nvidia is making PC gaming something only Trustafarians, doctors, lawyers, or cartel bosses can afford. If Intel keeps it up on the low end of decent sub-$300 cards, who are Nvidia's cards going to sell to? Oh, and this is at the FE MSRP of $999. Micro Center mailed out the prices of what they'll be selling 5080s for: $1150-$1350. Or you can buy an Xbox Series X for $500 and play Cyberpunk looking pretty good and afford an omelet.

Nvidia needs to use their AI riches to make gamer GPUs affordable again. They need to lower the tiers and prices to where the 3000-series cards were intended to be in Sept. 2020. x90s = $1500, x80s = $700, x70s = $500. Make the 5090 the $1500 card - heck, let's add a C-note for inflation - make it $1600, the 5080 $800, and the 5070 $550 (as it will be) with actual 30% uplifts and they'll make up in volume what they're losing in margin. It's not like dollar stores are going bankrupt, ya know?

Nvidia makes the best GPUs. Period. But as Paul said, the problem isn't the cards, it's what they're selling for and the value they deliver. It takes many hours, sometimes DAYS for Pixar to render a single frame of their movies and we expect near-Pixar quality, but at 200 fps at 4K with full ray tracing, but don't want to pay more than $500 for it. That's untenable. The fact they can do 30 fps is a miracle regardless of price. There has to be a compromise on both sides.

There is going to be a lot of negativity here - Understandable with the sentiment Paul expressed well of nVidia serving AI TechBros and shareholders with gamers coming last.

On the glass half full side, it seems their AI tech and frame gen tech may finally pay off for gamers on a budget with mid range cards.

As pointed out by Ancient GamePlays and some other YT reviewer channels, with DLSS4 the quality is better than native (because of inferiorTAA).
To add to this, in Cyberpunk on my 4070 ti super, I am getting 140+fps with DLSS-Q, RT Ultta (Path Tracing) and Frame Gen. I don't notice any input lag - It is smooth and responsive and looks waay better than native with regular RT.

Assuming Nvidia brings this to more games (which they will), this is a big win for consumers on mid range cards. DLSS4 will be supported on 20, 30 and 40 series cards (with FGx1 on 40 series)..

It strikes me that nVidia is the one delivering this value and benefit to consumers and AMD has consistently played catch up and only offers a slight discount for inferior tech.

My last few cards were Radeons and I recently switched to a 4070 ti super - So I did hang in there for a decade, but my patience wiith AMD playing follow the leader is wearing thin.

comments.text:
Okay Paul, I've been watching you more and more; perhaps will subscribe, but I wanted to let you know something I see that is lacking in these comparisons. And it is incredible that it is practically omitted on purpose by reviewers who absolutely adore charts. So, let's chart on and see what I'm talking about.

The GTX 980 was released in 2014 at $550. Okay. But that does not mean that such a card could ever sell for $550 if we had somehow just arrived at that level of technology. 
ENTER INFLATION!!
So 2014 had 1.6%, 2015 had 0.1%, 2016 had 1.3%, 2017 had 2.1%, 2018 had 2.4%, 2019 had 1.8%, 2020 had 1.2%, 2021 had 4.7%, 2022 had 8%, 2023 had 4.1%, and 2024 had 2.9%. 
Therefore, the GTX 980 in 2025 dollars cost $757. And already the numbers are WAY WAY OFF!!!!
The GTX 1080 in 2025 dollars cost $793.
The RTX 2080 in 2025 dollars cost $894.
The RTX 3080 in 2025 dollars cost $858.
The RTX 4080S in 2025 dollars cost $1029.
And the RTX 5080 costs $1000.

As you can see from actual reality, of what your dollars buy (regardless of the EXACTING numbers of the past, things always cost more) - and so the problem isn't the 5080 at all. It's the 4080. And even that could be just due to the fact that the 3080 was priced too low.

It would seem that a lack of basic economic theory is affecting the reviewers with regard to this latest card. I mean, all things being equal; do you really think that the 5080 is less of a bargain than the 4080S? And that's using your numbers? If the 5080 and the 4080S were both being sold right now for $1000. Would you think that that the 4080S made more sense?

See, this is the problem with the reviewers. They are emotionally invested, not intellectually invested. And I'm not talking about you personally. You are clear about it; saying that you are reporting what all other reviewers are saying. But really how many reviewers are we really talking about? And they are generally friends and speak to one another. So, that's the problem. This is an emotional expression. And I've shown the math. It is reasonable. NVIDIA has to keep raising the prices because they are not video card salesmen. They are beholden to their stock holders. THEY MUST INCREASE PRICES! That is the method of any and all technological companies in existence. They raise prices and keep their stock holders happy.

It is the fault of the consumers for continuing to purchase these cards no matter the cost.

But more importantly, it is the fault of a complete lack of competition. NVIDIA could charge $4000. People would still buy the 5090. They could charge $2000 for the 5080 and people would still buy it. NOBODY IS REMOTELY CLOSE!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

So, for a variety of reasons, I believe that all of these reviewers are out of touch with reality.

comments.text:
Paul, that chart you show at 4:00, can you do a version of that with die size included?

It used to be the 80 series was made on the top die, sometimes with some cores disabled (full fat version would be the TI or the 90 series). And then the next die down the stack would be much smaller and used for the 70 and 60 series.

But right now the 5080 is made on a tiny die that is less than 1/2 the size of what the 5090 brings to the table. In previous generations this would be the die that would have given us the 5070 and even the 5060, but instead we’re being told this is high end 4K gaming, and they want $1,000 for this micro (and I mean micro) chip. This chip is smaller than a 3060ti (which retailed at an overpriced $399) yet the price has gone up by 250%!

Meanwhile nVidia’s gross profit margins, as a percentage of sales are pushing toward 80% — meaning they’re making $1,000 revenue, and $800 gross profit, on every $200 of unit cost.

Gamers are getting ripped off. Plain and simple.

comments.text:
@Mewsashi-cz9fo  There are a couple of changes but ultimately minor:  now all the ALUs are capable of both 32 bit integer and 32 bit floating point operations.  The biggest benefit here is obviously code that uses lots of integer operations which could potentially double in throughput.  However for gaming that is relatively rare.  The second is better efficiency in scheduling operations since all the ALUs are uniform in capabilities. 

There is a newer on-die thread schedule for the GPU on the RTX 50 series.  Again, more of an efficiency play than a feature that directly improves theoretical performance.  This is analogous to Intel's thread scheduler in Alder/Raptor/Meteor/Arrow Lake products to manage their heterogenous architecture.

The last big change is the memory controller support for GDDR7 which offers a nice bandwidth boost over GDDR6X.  This does help with performance as the RTX 40 series could be bandwidth limited in some scenarios.

PCIe 5.0 support is here on the cards but an even bigger feature would be CXL support over PCIe 5.0   This is more of a workstation/server feature so we'll likely have to wait to and see if this actually in the silicon when the "Quadro" (but not named Quadro) cards arrive in a few months.   There are a handful of use cases for this to increase performance but would require some developer support to pull off.  Again, the potential performance gains with CXL would be isolated to those workstation/server applications, not gaming in general.
